decisions.quote: Objectives. To test whether a care management program could replicate its success in an earlier trial and determine likely explanations for why it did not.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree the study is a replication: it conducted a second randomized trial (Phase II, 2010-2014, N = 483 new high-risk enrollees) to test whether the Health Quality Partners (HQP) care management program could replicate the reductions in hospitalizations and Medicare expenditures achieved in Phase I (2002-2010).

decisions.quote: However, for the 15 percent of enrollees at high risk of hospitalization, the program reduced hospitalizations by an estimated 34 percent and Medicare expenditures (including monthly program fees) by 22 percent (Brown et al. 2012; Burwell 2014).
decisions.reason: The paper re-tests the Phase I HQP high-risk subgroup finding from the Medicare Coordinated Care Demonstration and explicitly cites both Brown et al. (2012) and Burwell (2014) for that original result (lines 58-61, 79-81). Brown et al. (2012) is the peer-reviewed journal article by the evaluation team reporting the original high-risk subgroup finding, whereas Burwell (2014) is the HHS Secretary's subsequent Report to Congress on the same evaluation (from which Table 2's Phase I summary column is drawn). Shipped coding of Brown et al. (2012) is supported by the text and pairs with blind target 0.

decisions.quote: From 2010 to 2014, the program did not reduce hospitalizations or generate Medicare savings to offset program fees that averaged $260 per beneﬁciary per month. These estimates are statistically different (p < .05) from the large reductions in hospitalizations and spending in the ﬁrst trial (2002–2010).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree that the replication outcome is 'failed'. The authors explicitly state that the Phase II program did not replicate its earlier Phase I success and did not reduce hospitalizations or Medicare expenditures.

decisions.quote: We tested whether the impact estimates for Phase II (using the primary sample) were statistically different from Phase I impacts for high-risk beneﬁciaries (N = 322), as reported in the evaluation’s ﬁfth report to Congress (Burwell 2014).
decisions.reason: Blind target 0 (Burwell 2014) is not an omitted independent original study; it is the government evaluation report for the same Phase I HQP trial already captured in shipped row 305 via the peer-reviewed article Brown et al. (2012).
